The final line suggests a turnaround in fortunes, as the speaker mentions someone who was previously in a relationship with someone else (“main ho”) but is now involved with the speaker (“fucking with Lone”). line: And my accountant say I’m bool Hit your accountant and they make the straight face right at you
vault_lines: And my accountant say I'm bool
meaning: In the line, “And my accountant say I’m bool / Hit your accountant and they make the straight face right at you”, Destroy Lonely is using wordplay to highlight the contrast between his own financial success and someone else’s potentially bad financial situation. The word “bool” is slang for “cool” or “good,” and in this context, it suggests that his accountant is approving or impressed by his financial standing—everything is in order and looking good. In the second part of the line, “Hit your accountant and they make the straight face right at you,” Lonely implies that if you were to check on another person’s accountant, they would likely have a serious or uncomfortable expression (the “straight face”) because things aren’t going well—there’s financial trouble or mismanagement. This contrast is a boast, showing that while his finances are in a strong position, the other person’s accountant might be facing a difficult situation, perhaps due to poor financial planning or a lack of success. Essentially, he’s flexing his wealth and financial stability while subtly calling out others for their potential financial struggles. Typical Lone.

line: Only way you’re cagin’ me is with Givenchy locks
vault_lines: Only way you're cagin' me is with Givenchy locks
meaning: In the line “Only way you’re cagin’ me is with Givenchy locks” from Destroy Lonely’s unreleased song Out The Box, he’s using a clever metaphor to express his independence and status. The phrase “cagin' me” suggests being trapped or controlled, but Lonely makes it clear that no one can confine him, except in the form of luxury—specifically, Givenchy locks. Givenchy, a high-end luxury brand known for its fashion and jewelry, often incorporates lock motifs into its designs, like padlock necklaces or bracelets, and by referencing this, Lonely is saying that the only way he could be “locked down” is through something as extravagant as designer jewelry. The line serves as both a flex on his wealth and an assertion of his untouchable lifestyle—he’s too free and powerful to be confined by anything but high-end fashion. It reinforces his image of being a fashionable, rebellious figure who is only constrained by luxury and excess.

line: (No stylist)
vault_lines: I'm in this bitch smoking dope right now
meaning:
In this rather sly adlib, Mr. Lonely foreshadows his big 2022 project, NO STYLIST. This adlib understandably flew over many fans' heads, likely because it was meant to be interpreted as such; a simple adlib. But in reality, he wanted to notify his loyal fans that he indeed, was working on a project called NO STYLIST, set to release in 2022.

Now the 2022 release date itself was not mentioned at all in this song, but if you examine closely, you’ll see that he also implied a 2022 release. Think back to the actual song title, “Layover”. This word has 7 letters in it. 7 is an odd number. Destroy Lonely has approximately 13 letters in it, in which 13 is also an odd number. 13 – 7 = 6. Coincidentally, “Lonely” also has 6 letters. This means that his name contains both odd and even numbers. The number 6 also corresponds to the month of June of 2020, which is the month this song released. 6/26/2020 is the release date for this song, and 6 + 26 + 2020 = 2052. The number 2 is in both the 1st and 4th position, and 1 and 4 are odd and even numbers. Put both of those 2’s together and you get 22. Coincidentally, NO STYLIST released in 2022. Therefore, Lonely predicted the release of his project in 2022.

Section 187 (often referred to in slang simply as 187) of the California Penal Code defines the crime of murder. The number is commonly pronounced by reading the digits separately as “one-eight-seven”, or “one-eighty-seven”, rather than “one hundred eighty-seven”.

The number “187” has been used by gangs throughout the United States and elsewhere as a synonym for murder; this usage has been documented in Florida, Wisconsin, the United Kingdom, Germany and Norway. It also features widely in hip-hop culture, such as in Dr. Dre’s “Deep Cover” or, YNW Melly’s “Murder on My Mind”.

Unidentified flying object (abbreviated as “UFO”) or unidentified anomalous phenomenon (abbreviated as “UAP”) is any aerially-controlled phenomenon that cannot be identified or defined as a registered or licensed aircraft via observation, radio towers or control towers.

line: Yeah, stupid bitch, I’m ballin’ hard’, might punch a nigga like I’m Ron Artest
vault_lines: Yeah, stupid bitch, I'm ballin' hard', might punch a nigga like I'm Ron Artest
meaning:
Lone is referencing the Malice at the Palace" which was a fight, involving both players and fans, that occurred during a NBA game between the Indiana Pacers and the defending champion Detroit Pistons on November 19, 2004, at The Palace in Auburn Hills, Michigan. The Associated Press called it “the most infamous brawl in NBA history.” With the Pacers leading 97–82 and 45.9 seconds left in the game, Pistons center Ben Wallace attempted a layup shot but was fouled from behind by Pacers small forward Ron Artest. A furious Wallace then shoved Artest, and a fight broke out on the court between a few players from both squads. The players had been separated, game officials were discussing consequences, and Artest was lying on the scorer’s table when a fan named John Green hit him with a drink thrown from several rows up in the stands.

Artest immediately charged into the crowd and grabbed another fan, Michael Ryan, whom he mistakenly believed was the culprit. Several Pacer teammates followed, more drinks and punches were thrown, and the incident escalated into a large brawl that spread from the stands to the court and involved fans and players from both teams. The game was never completed, as a massive police presence was called to the venue to restore order and, later, to allow the visiting Pacers to safely leave the building.

After the game, the NBA suspended nine players, including Artest and Wallace, for a total of 146 games, leading to the players losing $11 million in salary. Five players were charged with assault, and eventually sentenced to a year of probation and community service. Five fans also faced assault charges and were banned from attending Pistons home games for life. The fight also led the NBA to increase security between players and fans and limit the sale of alcohol at games.
